newsitem.title: ANTIGUA AND BARBUDA: Caribbean leaders brace for Lome pact changes.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean leaders brace for Lome pact changes.

text.p: Leaders of the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom), along with the presidents of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, met Thursday to prepare for negotiating a new Lome trade-and-aid accord with the European Union at a time when trade preferences may not last much longer.

The Lome IV accord is set to expire in 2000, and a green paper circulated by the European Union indicated the EU is considering making a number of radical changes to the Lome V accord, according to officials at the Caricom meeting.
The Caribbean is concerned that any such changes do not jeopardize the need for a stable transition for the region of tiny economies.
"Cooperation should combine subsidies, investment and trade with a gradual change toward liberalization," said Lionel Fernandez, president of the Dominican Republic, at the Thursday meeting.
The United States has challenged the region's special banana export arrangement with Europe before the World Trade Organization.

Washington dealt the Caribbean another blow when it persuaded the WTO to agree to include rum in any agreement on eliminating tariffs on distilled spirits. Regional rum producers enjoy special preferences in Europe, but the new WTO decision would phase out preferences ahead of the timetable agreed with the EU.

The EU banana regime in particular is critical to the four Windward Island states of the eastern Caribbean, accounting for as much as two-thirds of their total export earnings. Jamaica and Barbados have been the major beneficiaries under the rum protocol.

"In a sense, Lome has inhibited competition and development of a business environment of the recipient countries," Fernandez said. "Preferences have not worked to promote diversification...we need to remember that all trade preferences will be phased out and should be prepared to surrender (them) in return for improved aid, debt relief and soft loans."
But Fernandez's stance may not go down well with some Caricom countries, which have already rejected suggestions from Washington that it agree to end the banana regime in return for more aid.

One suggestion is that the Caribbean should attempt to negotiation a more reciprocal trade accord with the EU that would allow European exports to the region to expand only if Caribbean exports to the EU did so as well.
That would provide the EU with the incentive to offer aid designed to foster the development of more regional industries.
